claims.text: Incorporating aluminum into a TiVNbTa-based refractory high-entropy alloy will enable formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale.
The Al2O3 scale will improve high-temperature oxygen resistance by limiting oxygen ingress.
Limiting oxygen ingress will mitigate phase segregation and softening.
TiVNbTa is vulnerable to oxygen-associated phase segregation during aging at high temperature.
TiVNbTa progressively softens during aging at 700°C.
Adding 2–5 wt% aluminum will promote in situ Al2O3-scale formation during high-temperature exposure.
Oxygen-induced degradation of TiVNbTa has been observed under prolonged exposure in an oxygen-containing atmosphere at approximately 700°C.
A continuous, adherent alumina scale acts as a physical barrier that retards oxygen diffusion into the alloy bulk.
Aluminum in the RHEA will preferentially oxidize at high temperature.
Preferential aluminum oxidation will produce a stable, slow-growing alumina layer.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen interstitials promote phase segregation in TiVNbTa during thermal aging.
The aluminum-alloyed RHEA will develop a thinner and more uniform oxide scale than untreated TiVNbTa.
After oxidation exposure, the aluminum-alloyed RHEA will retain higher mechanical strength than untreated TiVNbTa.
After oxidation exposure, the aluminum-alloyed RHEA will show less phase segregation and degradation than untreated TiVNbTa.
Untreated TiVNbTa develops phase segregation and progressive softening during high-temperature aging.
The untreated alloy's segregation and softening are caused by uncontrolled oxygen ingress.
The protective effect is expected during sustained oxidation at around 700°C.
Changes in oxygen partial pressure, exposure duration, or temperature may alter alumina-scale behavior and protective efficacy.
